The history of the Roman Empire is a sprawling narrative of ambition, engineering, conquest, and eventual transformation, spanning over a millennium if one includes its Eastern continuation. It begins not with an empire, but with a small city-state on the banks of the Tiber River in central Italy. According to legend, Rome was founded in 753 BCE by the twins Romulus and Remus, though archaeological evidence suggests a gradual coalescence of Latin and Sabine villages during this period.

For its first two and a half centuries, Rome was ruled by kings, a period known as the Regal Era. These early rulers, a mix of Latin and Etruscan monarchs, laid the foundational infrastructure of the city, including the draining of the marshes to create the Forum Romanum and the construction of the Cloaca Maxima sewer system. However, the monarchy ended in 509 BCE following the overthrow of the tyrannical King Tarquin the Proud. This revolt sparked the birth of the Roman Republic, a system designed explicitly to prevent the return of single-man rule.

The Republic was characterized by a complex system of checks and balances, centered around the Senate, a body of aristocratic elders, and two annually elected consuls who held executive power. Over the next few centuries, Rome expanded its influence across the Italian peninsula through a combination of military prowess and diplomatic astuteness, often granting varying degrees of citizenship to conquered peoples to ensure loyalty. By the 3rd century BCE, Rome had come into conflict with Carthage, the dominant maritime power of the western Mediterranean. The ensuing Punic Wars, particularly the second led by the Carthaginian general Hannibal, tested Rome to its breaking point.
